---
title: "Partner-dependence checks for longitudinal data"
description: "False alarms, detection and fitting behavior for member-mean and same-occasion predictive checks."
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
    toc_float: true
    self_contained: true
params:
  output_directory: "../../dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/report-data/ild-partner-dependence"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 180, fig.retina = 1, out.width = "100%")
read_results <- function(filename) read.csv(file.path(params$output_directory, filename))
cells <- read_results("cells.csv")
flags <- read_results("flags.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell")
figures <- read_results("figures.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell")
fits <- read_results("fits.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell")
recovery <- read_results("recovery.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell")
effect_sizes <- read_results("effect-sizes.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell")
family_labels <- c(gaussian = "Gaussian", ar = "Gaussian + AR",
  poisson = "Poisson", ordinal = "Ordinal", lag_gaussian = "Gaussian + lags",
  lag_nbinom2 = "NB2 + lags")
model_labels <- c(no_occasion_covariance = "Omit occasion covariance",
  no_stable_covariance = "Omit stable covariance")
primary_flags <- flags |> filter(fits == "usable", rule == "rank")
primary_figures <- figures |> filter(fits == "usable", rule == "rank")
rate_interval <- function(rate, lower, upper) {
  sprintf("%.1f%% [%.1f, %.1f]", 100 * rate, 100 * lower, 100 * upper)
}
study_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
is_pilot <- any(cells$repetitions < 500 | cells$reference_draws < 1000)
```

## Summary

```{r summary-numbers}
percent_range <- function(rate) paste0(paste(unique(round(100 * range(rate))), collapse = "–"), "%")
null_rows <- primary_flags |>
  filter(statistic == "partner_cor",
    (truth_case == "zero_stable" & model == "no_stable_covariance" & level == "between") |
    (truth_case == "zero_occasion" & model == "no_occasion_covariance" & level == "within")) |>
  mutate(family = factor(part, names(family_labels), family_labels), dyads = factor(n_dyads))
covariance_rows <- primary_flags |>
  filter(part %in% c("gaussian", "poisson", "ordinal"), truth_case == "correlated",
    model %in% names(model_labels), statistic == "partner_cor") |>
  mutate(targeted = (model == "no_stable_covariance" & level == "between") |
    (model == "no_occasion_covariance" & level == "within"),
    family = factor(part, names(family_labels), family_labels),
    restriction = factor(model, names(model_labels), model_labels))
detection_rows <- covariance_rows |> filter(n_dyads == 200, n_occasions == 14, missing_share == 0)
targeted_detection <- detection_rows |> filter(targeted)
ar_unrestricted <- primary_figures |>
  filter(part == "ar", model == "no_ar", ar_phi == 0.7, figure == "either")
lag_figures <- primary_figures |> filter(startsWith(part, "lag_"), figure == "either")
small_detection <- covariance_rows |> filter(targeted, n_dyads == 50) |>
  slice_min(rate, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

The saved run targets `r unique(cells$repetitions)` datasets per setting and
`r unique(cells$reference_draws)` reference simulations per fitted model, across
`r nrow(cells)` settings. `r if (is_pilot) "**These are pilot results for checking the workflow. They do not establish calibration or detection rates.**" else "The results describe these simulated settings. They do not establish calibration for every supported model."`

- **Correct restrictions rarely flag.** When a fitted covariance restriction was
  true, the partner correlation it targets flagged in
  `r percent_range(null_rows$rate)` of datasets.
- **Omitted partner covariance shows at its level, given enough dyads.** It was
  detected in at least `r scales::percent(min(targeted_detection$rate), accuracy = 1)`
  of datasets with 200 dyads and 14 occasions, but in as few as
  `r scales::percent(small_detection$rate, accuracy = 1)` with 50 dyads and
  `r small_detection$n_occasions` occasions.
- **Omitted autocorrelation is not detected.** A model without AR, but with
  unrestricted covariances, flagged in
  `r scales::percent(max(ar_unrestricted$rate), accuracy = 1)` of datasets despite
  strong autocorrelation (φ = 0.7). Check autocorrelation separately.
- **Lagged outcomes as predictors can make the checks misleading.** Flag rates
  were `r percent_range(lag_figures$rate)`, depending on the family and on
  model-centring.

## What the study checks

[`check_partner_dependence(member = person, time = occasion)`](../reference/check_partner_dependence.html) compares the model's
simulations with the observed responses at two levels: **member means
(between)** and **deviations from those means on shared occasions (within)**.
This study asks how often these checks flag under correct covariance
restrictions, and what they detect when a restriction is wrong.

The fitted models have two partner covariances: a stable one between partners'
random intercepts, and an occasion one between their dyad-occasion random
effects. Each omission should show at its targeted level: the between level for
the stable covariance, and the within level for the occasion covariance.

A **row flag** means that one observed statistic (one row of the check's
`summary`) lies outside the middle 95% of its simulated values. Each level has
its own figure. A **figure flag** means that at least one row in that figure
flags. These are descriptive checks. The dashed 5% line in the false-alarm
figure is a benchmark for individual rows, not a promised rate or a figure-level
threshold. Summaries freely estimated from the
same data may flag much less often.

<details>
<summary>Design and interpretation</summary>

All settings use female-male dyads and the generator's fixed-effect terms,
including role intercepts and actor/partner predictors. Gaussian settings vary the
number of dyads (50 or 200), occasions (3, 5 or 14), and missingness (0% or 20%).
Poisson and ordinal settings use 50 or 200 dyads and 5 or 14 complete occasions.
AR and lagged-outcome settings use 50 or 200 dyads and 14 complete occasions.
Missing occasions are removed independently per member. A retained response
still contributes to its member's mean when the partner is missing. Non-lagged
actor/partner predictors are generated independently between partners at both levels.

Gaussian and Poisson models either retain both covariance blocks (the full model)
or set stable
or occasion partner covariance to zero. Ordinal outcomes have four categories,
a probit link and a shared dyad-occasion intercept instead of an unrestricted
occasion block. Separate settings make each covariance restriction true.
Additional Gaussian models impose equal occasion variances or omit AR(1)
dependence. Lagged-outcome Gaussian and NB2 fits are practical sensitivity
analyses: their predictors depend on earlier outcomes, so they are not clean
calibration controls.

Every reference simulation draws new random effects and responses, while keeping
fitted parameters and predictor values fixed. Models are not refitted. Checks
subtract the same fixed-effect predictions from observed and simulated responses
(model-centring). The lagged-outcome table also shows raw checks, which skip
this step.
Each dataset then supplies its own member means. Nonlinear links and short
series can let a misfit at one level affect summaries at the other.

Plots and tables below use fits with optimizer convergence, a positive-definite
Hessian and a finite log-likelihood. Gaussian models use BFGS, and other families
use `nlminb`. Failed fits are not retried. The saved tables also report all available
checks, including fits that fail those criteria, and preserve failures separately.

Error bars and brackets are 95% Wilson intervals for flag rates. Monte Carlo SEs
describe uncertainty from the number of generated datasets. Neither measures
uncertainty in an individual model's fitted parameters.

</details>

## False alarms under a true restriction

Here the fitted covariance restriction is true. Each panel shows the partner
correlation row at the targeted level: zero stable covariance at the
between level, or zero occasion covariance at the within level. Rates for other
rows remain in the saved tables. These true-restriction settings use complete
data and 5 or 14 occasions (only 14 for ordinal outcomes).

```{r true-restrictions, fig.alt="Partner-correlation flag rates under true zero-covariance restrictions, by family, level, number of occasions and dyad count."}
ggplot(null_rows, aes(n_occasions, rate, colour = dyads, group = dyads)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(family ~ level) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(5, 14)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Occasions", y = "Datasets with a row flag", colour = "Dyads") + study_theme
```

```{r false-alarm-findings, results='asis'}
if (!is_pilot) {
  null_figures <- primary_figures |>
    semi_join(null_rows, by = c("cell", "model", "response")) |> filter(figure == "either")
  full_figures <- primary_figures |> filter(model == "correct", figure == "either")
  gaussian_full <- full_figures |> filter(part == "gaussian")
  cat(sprintf("Under true zero-covariance restrictions, the partner-correlation row at the targeted level flagged in **%.1f–%.1f%%** of datasets. A flag anywhere in either figure occurred in **%.1f–%.1f%%**. For full models, either-figure rates were **%.1f–%.1f%%** across families and **%.1f–%.1f%%** for Gaussian models.\n\n",
    100 * min(null_rows$rate), 100 * max(null_rows$rate),
    100 * min(null_figures$rate), 100 * max(null_figures$rate),
    100 * min(full_figures$rate), 100 * max(full_figures$rate),
    100 * min(gaussian_full$rate), 100 * max(gaussian_full$rate)))
}
```

## Detection at both levels

These panels use 200 dyads, 14 complete occasions and nonzero partner covariance
at both levels. They show how omitting either covariance affects the partner
correlation row at **both** levels. A flag does not by itself locate the source
of the mismatch.

```{r omitted-covariance, fig.alt="Partner-correlation flag rates at both levels when stable or occasion covariance is omitted, with 200 dyads and 14 complete occasions."}
ggplot(detection_rows, aes(rate, restriction)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = restriction), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(family ~ level) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Datasets with a row flag", y = NULL) + study_theme
```

Response-scale correlations below describe the generated data after subtracting
their true fixed-effect means. They help distinguish response-scale dependence
from latent covariance parameters. These estimates use large complete samples.
They are not fitted-model results.

```{r response-effect-sizes}
effect_sizes |>
  filter(part %in% c("gaussian", "poisson", "ordinal"), truth_case == "correlated",
    n_dyads == 200, n_occasions == 14, missing_share == 0) |>
  transmute(Family = family_labels[part], Between = between_partner_cor,
    Within = within_partner_cor) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r main-findings, results='asis'}
if (!is_pilot) {
  small_stable <- covariance_rows |> filter(targeted, n_dyads == 50, level == "between")
  small_occasion <- covariance_rows |> filter(targeted, n_dyads == 50, level == "within")
  short_series <- small_occasion |> filter(part == "gaussian", n_occasions == 3) |>
    arrange(missing_share)
  cat(sprintf("With 200 dyads and 14 complete occasions, detection at the targeted level was **%.1f–%.1f%%**. At 50 dyads it was **%.1f–%.1f%%** for omitted stable covariance and **%.1f–%.1f%%** for omitted occasion covariance. In Gaussian data with 50 dyads and 3 occasions, occasion-covariance detection fell from **%.1f%%** with complete data to **%.1f%%** with 20%% missing member occasions.\n\n",
    100 * min(targeted_detection$rate), 100 * max(targeted_detection$rate),
    100 * min(small_stable$rate), 100 * max(small_stable$rate),
    100 * min(small_occasion$rate), 100 * max(small_occasion$rate),
    100 * short_series$rate[1], 100 * short_series$rate[2]))
  sd_rows <- primary_flags |> filter(part == "gaussian", model == "equal_occasion_variances",
    level == "within", statistic == "average_difference_cor")
  cat(sprintf("The partner-correlation row at the other level flagged at most **%.1f%%** across these covariance-omission settings. That result concerns this row, not every statistic or possible mismatch. In the Gaussian settings, where the two roles' true occasion SDs differ by a factor of 1.5, incorrectly imposing equal occasion variances was detected by the within-level dyad-average/role-difference correlation in **%.1f–%.1f%%** of datasets.\n\n",
    100 * max(covariance_rows$rate[!covariance_rows$targeted]),
    100 * min(sd_rows$rate), 100 * max(sd_rows$rate)))
}
```

## Serial dependence and lagged outcomes

Omitted autocorrelation raises two questions: does it cause false alarms for
other restrictions, and does the check reveal it? The generated data have AR(1)
dependence (φ = 0.7) or none (φ = 0, the control), and the models in this
section omit it. One model also imposes equal occasion variances for both roles,
which is true here. The table shows the row that checks this restriction: the
within-level dyad-average/role-difference correlation.

```{r ar-restriction}
ar_rows <- primary_flags |>
  filter(part == "ar", model == "no_ar_equal_occasion_variances", level == "within",
    statistic == "average_difference_cor") |>
  arrange(n_dyads, ar_phi)
ar_rows |>
  transmute(Dyads = n_dyads, `AR coefficient` = ar_phi, Checked = checked,
    `Flag rate [95% interval]` = rate_interval(rate, lower, upper),
    `Monte Carlo SE (%)` = round(100 * mcse, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r serial-dependence-finding, results='asis'}
if (!is_pilot) {
  ar_changes <- ar_rows |> select(n_dyads, ar_phi, rate, mcse) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = ar_phi, values_from = c(rate, mcse)) |>
    mutate(change = .data[["rate_0.7"]] - rate_0,
      change_mcse = sqrt(.data[["mcse_0.7"]]^2 + mcse_0^2))
  cat(sprintf("From φ = 0 to φ = 0.7, row-flag rates rose by **%.1f and %.1f percentage points** at 50 and 200 dyads (Monte Carlo SEs **%.1f and %.1f**, independent settings): small and imprecise increases. The variance equality is true, so the mismatch is the omitted serial dependence.\n\n",
    100 * ar_changes$change[1], 100 * ar_changes$change[2],
    100 * ar_changes$change_mcse[1], 100 * ar_changes$change_mcse[2]))
  if (all(ar_unrestricted$rate == 0))
    cat("The unrestricted covariance model without AR produced **no figure flags** at either sample size despite φ = 0.7. These summaries did not reveal the missing serial dependence. Autocorrelation needs a separate check.\n\n")
  if (file.exists(file.path(params$output_directory, "serial-recovery.csv"))) {
    serial_recovery <- read_results("serial-recovery.csv") |> left_join(cells, by = "cell") |>
      arrange(n_dyads)
    cat(sprintf("Yet the unrestricted model without AR underestimated the stable partner correlation: **%.3f and %.3f** on average at 50 and 200 dyads, versus a true **%.2f** (Monte Carlo SEs **%.3f and %.3f**).\n\n",
      serial_recovery$mean[1], serial_recovery$mean[2], serial_recovery$true_value[1],
      serial_recovery$mcse[1], serial_recovery$mcse[2]))
  }
}
```

These checks can be misleading when the model includes lagged outcomes as predictors.
For these models, simulations keep the observed lag predictors fixed.
The following table compares raw and model-centred checks using the same
simulations. It reports a flag **anywhere in either figure**. High rates can
reflect this simulation limitation as well as fitting behavior. They are not
false-alarm estimates for a clean null model.

```{r lag-sensitivity}
lag_figures |>
  arrange(part, n_dyads, response) |>
  transmute(Family = family_labels[part], Dyads = n_dyads, Response = response,
    Checked = checked, `Any flag [95% interval]` = rate_interval(rate, lower, upper),
    `Monte Carlo SE (%)` = round(100 * mcse, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Low model-centred flag rates in the Gaussian lagged-outcome case do not establish
that keeping outcome-derived predictors fixed gives a valid simulation reference.

## Fitting and sensitivity checks

The denominator of each rate is the number of datasets for which that check was
available in the stated fit subset. Each table row counts one family's models
across all settings. A single generated dataset may supply several fitted models.

```{r fit-availability}
fits |>
  summarise(Attempted = sum(attempted), Usable = sum(usable),
    `Optimizer failures` = sum(not_converged), `Hessian problems` = sum(not_positive_hessian),
    `Fit errors` = sum(fit_errors), `Check errors` = sum(check_errors), .by = part) |>
  mutate(Family = family_labels[part], .before = 1) |>
  select(-part) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r rule-and-fit-sensitivity, results='asis'}
rule_comparison <- flags |>
  filter(fits == "usable") |>
  select(cell, model, response, level, statistic, rule, rate) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = rate)
fit_comparison <- flags |>
  filter(rule == "rank") |>
  select(cell, model, response, level, statistic, fits, rate) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = fits, values_from = rate)
cat(sprintf("Flags use rank limits from the ordered simulated values, as `check_partner_dependence()` does. Interpolated quantiles would change per-row rates by at most **%.1f percentage points**. The largest difference between all available checks and usable fits was **%.1f percentage points**, among rows available in both subsets.\n\n",
  100 * max(abs(rule_comparison$quantile - rule_comparison$rank), na.rm = TRUE),
  100 * max(abs(fit_comparison$all - fit_comparison$usable), na.rm = TRUE)))
```

Apart from the AR result above, parameter recovery is kept separate from check
performance. The saved recovery
table contains estimates only for correctly specified models, excluding the
lagged-outcome sensitivity fits. This compact view gives the largest absolute
bias across settings for fixed predictor effects and latent partner correlations.

```{r parameter-recovery}
parameter_labels <- c(x_actor = "Actor effect", x_partner = "Partner effect",
  block1_cor = "Stable correlation", block2_cor = "Occasion correlation")
recovery |>
  filter(parameter %in% names(parameter_labels)) |>
  summarise(`Largest absolute bias` = max(abs(bias)),
    `Fewest usable estimates` = min(n), .by = c(part, parameter)) |>
  transmute(Family = family_labels[part], Parameter = parameter_labels[parameter],
    `Largest absolute bias`, `Fewest usable estimates`) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The [full tables](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/tree/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/report-data/ild-partner-dependence)
retain all statistics, missingness settings, sample sizes,
figure-level rates and Monte Carlo SEs. See the
[study code](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/ild-partner-dependence/run.R),
[design](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/ild-partner-dependence-plan.md#7-validation-after-implementation-once)
and [run instructions](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/README.md#longitudinal-partner-dependence-checks).
